meeting_header: Date: 2026-03-10 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Ramos (Redwood) — Nina Patel, Samir Khan, Olivia Brooks (Arboria)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on unit economics. Reviewed tokens-per-dollar across model/quantization variants, observed KV-prefix caching savings, and discussed batching tradeoffs versus latency SLOs. Agreed next steps: run three-cache configs, share updated cost model, and validate cold starts on customer's infra.
topics: tokens/sec per dollar measurement and normalization
KV / prefix caching observed savings and limits
batching size vs latency SLO (p99) tradeoffs
dedicated vs hosted routing economics and reserved capacity scenarios
transcript: 00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining. we wanted to keep this tight — 40ish minutes — focus on the econ numbers and the cache experiment results
00:12 Nina Patel: yep that works, quick note we had a spike in token usage last night during batch ingestion, so excited to hear the numbers

00:20 Diego Ramos: okay we'll start with the baseline — our measurement uses tokens per dollar normalized to your pilot config (seq 256 average, batch windows 50ms); same infra assumptions as last week
00:36 Samir Khan: quick q, are you normalizing for prompt vs completion tokens? we saw prompts are heavy in our flow
00:44 Diego Ramos: good point — yes we separate prompt/completion; the tokens/$ metric we showed was combined but the sheet has both columns, I can re-export just completion-centric next time
01:05 Olivia Brooks: there was a note in slack about q4_0 causing hallucinations in some of our prompts — did you see quality regressions with quantized runs?

01:16 Diego Ramos: we ran q4_0 and q8_0 profiles; q4_0 saved ~3.8x tokens/$ versus fp16 but we saw small probability shifts on the narrow prompt set — not catastrophic but detectable on the safety prompts
01:32 Nina Patel: hmm okay. for us precision on transaction extraction is higher priority than raw cost, so maybe a hybrid approach

01:40 Maya Chen: exactly — many customers run a hybrid: routing cheap quantized model for standard queries and a higher fidelity model for edge cases. Redwood's routing policy can do that automatically per rule
01:57 Samir Khan: about the KV cache results — the spreadsheet says 27% token reduction when prefix caching is enabled? can you walk through that number

02:08 Diego Ramos: yes, the 27% is average across the 48-hour wiggle. important caveat — it was with a 30-minute TTL and assuming 60% repeat query overlap. cold-starts see almost no benefit until cache warms
02:29 Olivia Brooks: so in short, warm state saves ~25-30% tokens, cold starts zero — that matches what we see in prod traces
02:36 Maya Chen: also note prefix vs full KV difference: prefix cache gives more hits for partial prompts, but it's sensitive to tokenization changes, so you'll want canonicalization rules
02:49 Samir Khan: canonicalization — yes we've got a preproc step but it sometimes drops punctuation differently across languages
03:02 Diego Ramos: another config we tried was batching window tuning. raising window to 100ms increased tokens/sec/$ by about 12% but p99 latency regressed by ~90ms in our test harness
03:20 Nina Patel: 90ms p99 hit could be material for user-facing APIS — our SLA target is 350ms p99, what's your p99 baseline on the hosted pilot?

03:29 Maya Chen: hosted pilot baseline p99 was ~280ms with 50ms batch window and dynamic batching. With 100ms we were at 370ms, so that's why we recommend caution on increasing batch windows unless you have relaxed SLOs
03:45 Olivia Brooks: question on tokens/sec/$ — is that metric factoring in reserved capacity discounts or raw on-demand list prices?
03:54 Diego Ramos: good question — the numbers we shared in the deck were both: raw on-demand and a reserved 12-month commit scenario. reserved reduces effective $/token by ~22% in our config
04:08 Samir Khan: can you send the reserved vs burst scenarios in one sheet? it's hard to compare across multiple tabs
04:15 Maya Chen: yes that's on my list — I'll consolidate into one pivot view and add a sensitivity slider for percent cache hit and average seq length
04:27 Nina Patel: any notes about private deployment (VPC) overhead? Olivia is worried about egress + peering adding latency
04:35 Olivia Brooks: yep, our infra team measured ~18ms extra for peered traffic in dev — is that consistent with what Redwood sees?

04:42 Diego Ramos: peering typically adds 10-25ms depending on path; we try to compensate with local model variants and region routing. Also dedicated pools reduce variability though not raw latency by much
04:55 Samir Khan: you mentioned routing by policy — could we do cost-first routing during non-peak hours and latency-first during peak?
05:02 Maya Chen: absolutely, routing policies can be time-based and traffic-aware. many customers run cost-first for batch jobs and latency-first for interactive queries
05:12 Nina Patel: about the cache experiment — Diego can you explain the three configs briefly?
05:18 Diego Ramos: yes: config A = no prefix caching, TTL 0; config B = prefix caching enabled, TTL 30m; config C = prefix caching + adaptive TTL (shorten for low-hit keys). We ran 24h for each
05:33 Olivia Brooks: results looked promising for B except some keys caused cache churn — that's where adaptive TTL might help
05:40 Diego Ramos: right, adaptive TTL reduced churn in the run and kept effective hit rate higher by ~4 points which translated to another ~3% tokens/$ improvement
05:52 Samir Khan: small improvement but together adds up. what's the cost of storage and lookup ops for the cache? storage ops might cost more depending on provider
06:01 Diego Ramos: storage cost was negligible in our pilot scale; lookup ops were the main overhead but those are amortized across hits. we included them in tokens/$ denom as a small fixed cost
06:12 Nina Patel: are there any regression alerts for quality when caching is aggressive? e.g., stale KV leading to wrong completions

06:20 Diego Ramos: we've seen rare stale cases — that's why we recommend TTLs and key invalidation on inferred schema changes. also we log quality deltas to evals so we can rollback if regression > threshold
06:34 Olivia Brooks: about the evaluation — can we get the per-prompt quality diffs? it's easier to sign off if we see the exact prompts where q4_0 diverged
06:42 Maya Chen: yes Diego will attach the per-prompt diff CSV to the shared drive. note that q8_0 tended to have much smaller diffs than q4_0 in our tests
06:58 Samir Khan: how reproducible are the tokens/sec/$ numbers day-to-day? our traffic has a skewed time-of-day distribution

07:06 Diego Ramos: they fluctuate with sequence length and hit rate. we've included a sensitivity chart in the cost model showing 10-90th percentile scenarios; I'll surface the hourly breakdown as well
07:20 Nina Patel: switching topics — any blockers on your side to spin up a dedicated pool for our POC?
07:28 Maya Chen: for Redwood Dedicated we need a capacity window and commitment; Olivia can confirm peering & security—they usually sign a 3-month pilot reserved commit for stable perf
07:38 Olivia Brooks: we need procurement approval but infra is fine with a 3-month. what's the minimum monthly commit?
07:45 Maya Chen: we provided three tiers in the proposal; the lower tier covers your baseline test traffic and gives ~18% cost savings vs hosted on-demand when reserved
07:56 Samir Khan: could you share the proposal link in chat?
08:02 Maya Chen: yes I'll drop it in the meeting notes, will include a simple comparison table

08:10 Diego Ramos: quick mention of fallback policies — if dedicated capacity is saturated, Redwood can fallback to hosted variants with automatic model mapping to avoid failure. There's an observable cost delta when that happens
08:25 Nina Patel: that's reassuring. can we get alerting when fallback occurs? we need visibility into when we lose reserved performance
08:31 Diego Ramos: yes, audit logs and fallback alerts can go to your pager or slack channel; we'll work with Olivia to set up routing
08:45 Olivia Brooks: about security — we did review SOC2 docs last week, procurement asked for KMS key control details again
08:52 Maya Chen: we'll re-share the KMS/HSM section and operational runbook for private deployment. Diego will include the exact API for key rotation
09:05 Samir Khan: let's return to batching tradeoffs — do you have advice on dynamic batch sizing? our current logic uses a fixed 64 token budget per batch

09:15 Diego Ramos: dynamic batching that respects a hard p99 cap works well: set an upper latency cap and allow small batches to flush early. That often preserves p99 while getting most of the batching benefit
09:28 Nina Patel: do you have a rule-of-thumb mapping batch window to p99 delta?
09:33 Diego Ramos: roughly, increasing window by 50ms gave us ~8-12% tokens/$ in tests but increased p99 by 60-100ms depending on model size. the larger the model, the larger the p99 penalty
09:50 Samir Khan: so for us with a 350ms p99 target, 50ms window seems sweet spot
09:57 Maya Chen: sounds like we keep 50ms for interactive paths, try 100ms for batch jobs. Diego will run a 100ms batch experiment with your traffic profile next run
10:08 Olivia Brooks: what about traceability — we need per-token cost breakdown in traces for billing audits
10:15 Diego Ramos: Redwood Console can emit token-level attributes per request and aggregate to per-route dashboards; we'll enable that on the POC route and send sample exports
10:26 Nina Patel: great. any surprises in the data this week?
10:30 Diego Ramos: main surprise was one hot key that inflated cache churn — Samir's team identified the upstream canonicalization bug which when fixed improved hit rate by ~7%
10:41 Samir Khan: yeah that was my fault, we had a newline trim mismatch. fixed in staging, will promote to pilot after validation

10:49 Maya Chen: excellent — small fixes like that compound quickly. ok final recap: Diego runs KV 3-config runs and batching 100ms experiment; Maya sends consolidated cost pivot and proposal link; Samir validates cold-starts and shares histograms; Olivia confirms peering/fwall window
11:10 Nina Patel: thanks everyone, schedule same time next week?
11:15 Maya Chen: same time next week works — I'll send calendar invite and include the action items. thanks all
11:22 [meeting ends]
